wine.name: Santa Florentina Torrontés Riojano
wine.grapes: Torrontés Riojano alone, by the house's sheet.
wine.sites: Vineyards of the co-operative's grower families in the Famatina valleys around Chilecito, a hot, dry trough between the Sierra de Famatina and the Sierra de Velasco.
wine.making: By the house's sheet the juice is settled cold for a day or more, then fermented at a controlled 16 to 18 degrees Celsius with a selected local yeast of the co-operative's own, which keeps the grape's scent; the sheet names no oak, and the wine is bottled young.
wine.glass: Pale yellow with a green glint; orange blossom over grapefruit, apple and melon, with peach and pineapple behind, by the house's own note, dry, with fresh acidity under the scent.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two of the harvest, while the blossom scent is fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with a tulip bowl to gather the scent.

label.means: The pale skinned grape named for the province, the Torrontés of La Rioja rather than of San Juan or Mendoza.
The Famatina valleys around Chilecito, the province's main vineyard zone and the source of the grapes.
The co-operative's range of varietal and sparkling wines, sharing its name with a hamlet west of Chilecito.

records.table: La Riojana is the grower co-operative of Chilecito, at work since 1940, and Santa Florentina Torrontés Riojano is its varietal white of the Famatina valleys: orange blossom, grapefruit and melon, dry and fresh. Pour it cold, and pour it young.
records.story: La Riojana tells its own beginning this way: in 1940 a group of co-operative growers from Colonia Caroya, the Italian settlement in Córdoba with its own co-operative winery, La Caroyense, saw what the Famatina valleys could grow and settled a branch at Chilecito with growers of La Rioja. The co-operative of small and middling grower families that came of it presses a large share of the province's grapes, and Torrontés Riojano, the white grape named for the province, has always been its main wine. The two co-operatives worked as one for some fifty years, until La Riojana stood alone from 30 June 1989. In 2006 it was certified by Fairtrade, and the premium paid on those sales built a secondary school at Tilimuqui, near the cellar, opened in 2010. Santa Florentina, the house's range of varietal and sparkling wines, shares its name with a hamlet west of Chilecito where, early in the twentieth century, a smelter worked the ore carried down from the Famatina mines by the cable way from La Mejicana; its ruins stand there yet. To a sommelier the Santa Florentina Torrontés is the plain statement of the province's grape, made by growers rather than an estate, and a fair measure of Famatina Torrontés before any single vineyard name is added.

others.name: Tilimuqui Organic Torrontés
others.note: The co-operative's organic Fairtrade range from the Famatina, named for the village near the cellar where the school stands.

others.name: Santa Florentina Torrontés Riojano Chardonnay
others.note: A blend of the two grapes in the same range, Torrontés the larger part, in shares the house has changed over the years.

traps: La Rioja in Argentina shares only a name with Rioja in Spain; Santa Florentina is a white of the Famatina valleys, not a Spanish wine.
Torrontés Riojano is one of three Argentine grapes called Torrontés, with Torrontés Sanjuanino and Torrontés Mendocino; Riojano on the label names the one of this province.
Santa Florentina and Tilimuqui are both ranges of La Riojana; Tilimuqui is the organic one.

cards.front: La Riojana: in what year does the co-operative date its work at Chilecito?
cards.back: 1940, when growers from Colonia Caroya in Córdoba settled a branch in the Famatina valleys.

cards.front: What does the name Santa Florentina on a La Riojana label recall?
cards.back: A hamlet west of Chilecito where a smelter once worked the ore of the Famatina mines.

questions.q: A guest asks what grape makes La Riojana's Santa Florentina Torrontés. Which answer fits the house's sheet?
questions.exp: The house's sheet gives Torrontés Riojano alone, the province's own Torrontés; the range's blend with Chardonnay is a different wine.

questions.q: What did the Fairtrade premium earned by La Riojana build at Tilimuqui, opened in 2010?
questions.exp: The premium paid on Fairtrade sales built a secondary school at Tilimuqui, which took its first pupils in March 2010 and was inaugurated in May; the cellar itself stands at Chilecito.

La Riojana: Institucional and Santa Florentina pages
Fairtrade Foundation: La Riojana Cooperative
Bichos de Campo: La Riojana, the Chilecito co-operative
Argentina, Ministry of Culture: Cable Carril Chilecito to La Mejicana

report: 1940 and the start as an offshoot of the Colonia Caroya co-operative La Caroyense rest on the house's own institutional page and Bichos de Campo; Cadena 3 gives 1930 in one passage, which no other source repeats.

The grape, the zone (Valles de Famatina), the cold settling, the ferment at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius and the tasting note come from the house's own Santa Florentina Torrontés Riojano page, read through search.

Fairtrade in 2006 and the school at Tilimuqui in 2010 rest on the house and the Fairtrade Foundation; the house's claim to be the first Argentine winery certified is cut, as the lint asks for two sources of a first.

The house's page describes Santa Florentina as the hamlet of the Famatina smelter and gives the same name to its range; no source says in so many words that the range was named for it, so the record says it shares the name.

Member numbers (290, 360, 400, 500 by source) and the share of the province's crop (half by one source, near seventy per cent by another) are left out as volatile and unsettled; a large share is said instead.
The region record's producers line calls La Riojana the province's biggest producer and one of the world's leading Fairtrade wine sources; the record keeps no ranking.

changed: story: added that the two co-operatives worked as one for some fifty years until La Riojana stood alone from 30 June 1989, by the co-operative's own account and Economía Solidaria; 1940 and the branch of La Caroyense confirmed by Economía Solidaria and Rutacoop.

questions[1].exp: 'with help from buyers abroad' cut as unsourced; now the school took its first pupils in March 2010 and was inaugurated in May, by the house's Fairtrade page and Wines of Argentina's news of 28 May 2010.

sources[4]: Wikipedia's Santa Florentina page replaced by the national heritage page for the Chilecito to La Mejicana cable way, which names the Santa Florentina smelter the ore was carried to (a primary body).
open: The house says the range is named for the village twelve kilometres from its winery (la-riojana.squarespace.com, read through search); the record keeps 'shares its name', which is true and modest. The read together agent may let it say 'named for'.

records.place: Chañarmuyo, Famatina department, Famatina Valley, La Rioja

wine.name: Chañarmuyo Estate Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec, bottled as a varietal from the estate's own vines.
wine.sites: The estate's vineyards in the Chañarmuyo valley at the north of the Famatina, at about 1,700 metres, a desert valley by the house's account, watered from snowmelt through drip lines, with a swing of more than twenty degrees between day and night.
wine.making: Fermented and raised at the estate; the house's sheets for its varietal Malbec give eight months in oak on one page and twelve on another, and a merchant's sheet for the Estate bottling speaks only of a touch of oak, so the wood frames the fruit rather than leads. The sheets read give no detail of the ferment.
wine.glass: Ruby coloured; cherry and ripe plum with violet and a fresh note of mint, by the house's own notes, a light smoky touch from the wood, soft tannin and lively acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to drink in its first few years from the vintage, while the fruit and the violet scent are fresh.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though an hour in a carafe does no harm; a red wine glass of middle size.

label.means: The valley, the village and the estate's name, at the north of the Famatina in the province of La Rioja.
Wine of the house's own vineyards in the valley, as the label sold abroad names it.
The single variety named, the red grape Argentina is known by.

records.table: Bodega Chañarmuyo grows its Estate Malbec at about 1,700 metres in a desert valley at the north of the Famatina, an estate begun only in 2001. It shows cherry, plum and violet with a fresh note of mint, and it wants red meat from the grill.
records.story: Chañarmuyo is a small village in the Famatina department of La Rioja, in a valley with water but, by the account of Wines of Argentina, fewer than a hundred people when the estate began. The house dates its start to the end of 2001, when its founder bought land in the valley, and Wines of Argentina tells the project as one meant to bring work back to the village. By two academic studies of the province's wine, the estate was making and selling its own wine from 2006. The house tells a story older than its vines: a cross has looked down on the valley since 1913, and a villager of long ago is said to have foretold that wine would one day be made there, a tale the house itself offers as a legend it cannot prove. In 2014 the national wine institute recognised Valle de Chañarmuyo as a geographical indication of its own, by its resolution 28 of that year, and the estate built a small wine hotel within the cellar. To a sommelier the Estate Malbec is a lesson in height: a red from about 1,700 metres in a province better known for Torrontés, grown where the nights are cold enough to keep its acidity and its violet scent.

others.name: Chañarmuyo Reserva Malbec
others.note: The house's Reserva Malbec, listed by merchants beside the Estate bottling.

others.name: Chañarmuyo Gran Malbec
others.note: The house's Gran Vino Malbec, given eighteen months in French oak by its sheet.

others.name: Chañarmuyo Chardonnay
others.note: A white from the same desert valley, which the house's sheet places above 1,700 metres.

traps: Chañarmuyo lies in the Famatina department at the north of the valley, not at Chilecito, and its vines grow far higher than the co-operative growers' around the town.
Bodega Chañarmuyo has no tie to Spain's Rioja: La Rioja here is the Argentine province, and its valley has been a geographical indication of its own, Valle de Chañarmuyo, since 2014.

cards.front: Bodega Chañarmuyo: at about what height does its Estate Malbec grow?
cards.back: About 1,700 metres, in the Chañarmuyo valley at the north of the Famatina.

cards.front: When does Bodega Chañarmuyo date its start, and how?
cards.back: The end of 2001, when its founder bought land in the Chañarmuyo valley.

questions.q: A guest asks why Chañarmuyo's Estate Malbec keeps its freshness in a hot, dry province. Which reason fits?
opts: Vines at about 1,700 metres with cold nights
Grapes bought in from cool Patagonia
A long ferment in open clay jars
A large share of Torrontés in the blend
questions.exp: The estate's vines grow at about 1,700 metres, where the swing between day and night exceeds twenty degrees; the wine is a varietal Malbec, not a blend with Torrontés.

questions.q: In which year does Bodega Chañarmuyo date its start, when its founder bought land in the valley?
questions.exp: The house dates its start to the end of 2001; 1913 is the year of the cross that the house says has looked down on the valley.

sources.title: Bodega Chañarmuyo: Our story and Origin
Bodega Chañarmuyo: Malbec and Clásicos pages, terroir and technical sheets
Wines of Argentina: Bodega Chañarmuyo, the adventure of a viticultural dream
Instituto Nacional de Vitivinicultura: Resolución 28 of 2014, Valle de Chañarmuyo
Chain Bridge Cellars: Chañarmuyo Malbec Estate Grown 1700 MSNM

report: The start at the end of 2001 rests on the house's own story page and a wine tourism directory; 2006 for the first wine sold rests on two academic papers (RIVAR, the plan's note, and a UAM paper read through search) and is told as theirs.
Height: the house's sheet says more than 1,700 metres and Wine Folly 1,720; the record gives about 1,700.

The Estate label name rests on Delectable and a merchant's page; the house's own site sells its Malbec under the Clásicos line and was not seen to use the word Estate, so the integrator may wish to confirm the label as the bottle has it.
The house's two Malbec pages give eight and twelve months in oak with differing figures, so the making field gives a range and no single figure.
The founder is living and is not named; the house's prophet of the valley, a villager it names, is described because his dates were not found.

The national tourism board names the Tannat of the Gran Vino Reserva line as the most awarded wine; awards are never told, and no source read names a single flagship, so the Estate Malbec stands as the wine merchants abroad list most often.
No Torrontés from the estate was confirmed; the region record's producers line speaks of the estate's Torrontés and Malbec, and the record names no Torrontés.

changed: story, table, cards[1], questions[1]: the start at the end of 2001 was told as the family beginning to plant; the sources (vinosypasiones, the house) say the founder bought the land then, and planting is given as 2002 by one sheet and the first vines or harvest as 2005 by others, so now the founder bought land in the valley, and the table says an estate begun in 2001.

story: added the national wine institute's recognition of Valle de Chañarmuyo as a geographical indication by resolution 28 of 2014 (the resolution's text on argentina.gob.ar, and the INV's list of indications of April 2024); the national tourism board's listing of the hotel cut to make room, the hotel kept.
traps[1]: 'its wine is labelled for the Famatina valley' was unconfirmed; now the valley's own indication since 2014.
wine.making: 'some eight to twelve months' now eight months on one page and twelve on another, as the house's two Malbec sheets give them.
sources[3]: Argentina Travel replaced by the INV resolution 28 of 2014.

sources[4]: Delectable's address carries the living founder's surname, so it is replaced by a merchant listing of the bottle as Chañarmuyo Malbec Estate Grown 1700 MSNM, which also confirms the Estate label words.
open: wine.appellation: Valle de Famatina, La Rioja is the author's, and one merchant listing gives Valle de Famatina; whether the label prints Valle de Chañarmuyo, the indication of 2014, was not seen. A merchant gives 'Estate Grown 1700 MSNM' on the bottle. Confirm from a label.
2006 for the first wine sold rests on the author's two academic papers; one press piece gives a first harvest of 2005. Left as the papers' account.
The plan's why says 'planted from 2001'; the read together agent may set it to begun in 2001.

records.place: Aminga valley, Castro Barros department, La Rioja

wine.name: San Huberto Torrontés
wine.grapes: Torrontés, from the house's La Rioja vineyards.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards in the Aminga valley of the department of Castro Barros, on the eastern side of the Sierra de Velasco, away from the Famatina valleys, at about 1,450 metres by a trade fair listing of the firm.
wine.making: No technical sheet for this wine was found in the sources read, so the record gives no ferment, vessel or time; the house presents it as a varietal Torrontés of La Rioja, made to be sold young.
wine.glass: The sources read hold no tasting note from the house or a critic for this wine, so none is given here; taste the vintage poured before describing it to a guest, and name only what is in the glass.
wine.ageing: A young white, like the province's Torrontés in general: open it within a year or two of the vintage on the label.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with a tulip bowl.

label.means: The province of origin, in north west Argentina, and not the Spanish region of the same name.
The firm with a cellar in La Rioja's Aminga valley and another at Vistalba in Mendoza.

records.table: Bodegas San Huberto makes wine in two provinces, and its Torrontés comes from its La Rioja vineyards in the Aminga valley, east of the Sierra de Velasco. Ask which bottling the list holds, since the house sells Mendoza wines as well.
records.story: San Huberto is a house of two provinces. Its La Rioja cellar stands in the Aminga valley of the department of Castro Barros, on the eastern side of the Sierra de Velasco, and its second Argentine cellar is at Vistalba, in Luján de Cuyo in Mendoza. Directories of Argentine wineries trace its history to 1905, though they do not say where it began. An academic case study follows the firm's growth at Anillaco, in the same department of La Rioja, from 1998 to 2023, and notes its place within a long established Argentine business group. By the firm's own account in the press it bought a cellar at Huailai, north of Beijing, in 2001, and from 2002 the Chinese house Changyu has imported and sold San Huberto wines in China. Its labels name the valley as well as the province: the Nina wines of Valle de Aminga, and Aminga, a red the house calls its emblem. For a sommelier the San Huberto Torrontés is a white of the province from outside the Famatina valleys, and a reminder to read which province a San Huberto label names before pouring it as a wine of La Rioja.

others.name: Nina Torrontés, Valle de Aminga
others.note: A Torrontés of the house's Nina range, labelled for the Aminga valley.

others.name: Aminga
others.note: A red blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in American oak, by the house's account in the press.

traps: San Huberto makes wine in Mendoza as well as La Rioja; only a label that names La Rioja or Aminga is a wine of the province.
Aminga and Anillaco are towns of the same department, Castro Barros, on the far side of the Sierra de Velasco from Chilecito and the Famatina.

cards.front: Bodegas San Huberto: in which valley of La Rioja does its cellar stand?
cards.back: The Aminga valley, in the department of Castro Barros.

cards.front: Besides La Rioja, where in Argentina does Bodegas San Huberto have a cellar?
cards.back: At Vistalba, in Luján de Cuyo, Mendoza.

questions.q: A San Huberto label names a valley. Which valley name marks a wine of its La Rioja cellar rather than its Mendoza one?
questions.exp: Valle de Aminga, as the Nina wines print it, is the Castro Barros valley of the house's La Rioja cellar; Uco is in Mendoza, Tulum in San Juan and Calchaquí in Salta.

questions.q: By the Argentine press, which Chinese house has imported and sold San Huberto wines in China since 2002?
questions.exp: Forbes Argentina and Enolife give Changyu, which began importing the wines in 2002; Great Wall is another large Chinese house with no such tie in the sources read.

sources.title: Wine Folly Argentina guide: Bodegas San Huberto
RIVAR: case study of Bodegas San Huberto at Anillaco
Forbes Argentina: San Huberto strengthens its alliance with Changyu
ProWein 2022 Argentina pavilion: San Huberto
Enolife: Changyu brings a wine to Argentina in alliance with San Huberto

report: The thinnest record in sourcing after Vista Larga: no house site was found by search (sanhuberto.com.ar and like domains gave nothing), and the RIVAR case study could not be fetched (the host does not resolve here), so the making and the glass say plainly that no sheet or note was found.

The two cellars (Aminga valley, Castro Barros; Vistalba, Luján de Cuyo) rest on Wine Folly, Winetourism and the ProWein page; the RIVAR study places the firm at Anillaco, Aminga's neighbour in the same department, so the record names the valley and both towns.
1905 rests on two directory pages that may share one text; it is told as the directories' date and founded is left empty.
2002 for Changyu rests on Forbes Argentina alone, with iProfesional confirming the alliance but not the year; a refuter may cut the year and the second question if no second source is found.
The height of about 1,450 metres rests on one trade fair listing and is hedged as such; the owning group is named by two sources but left out as current ownership.

Swap to weigh: the house's own La Rioja white with a valley name is the Nina Torrontés, Valle de Aminga, which a critic's site lists; if the checker prefers a wine that names its valley, Nina Torrontés would be the truer pick, though the label now in the plan, San Huberto La Rioja Torrontés, is listed by Wine.com.
The wine's grape is given as Torrontés, not Torrontés Riojano, because no source read names the variety on this label.

changed: story: 'the firm also makes wine at Huailai' now 'by the firm's own account in the press it bought a cellar at Huailai in 2001', as its president told the press in 2023 (Enolife, El Cronista) and the RIVAR study notes the Huailai unit.
story, questions[1]: Changyu from 2002 now rests on Forbes Argentina and Enolife, so the stem says the Argentine press rather than Forbes alone.

story, others[1]: 'an Aminga range' was wrong in kind: Aminga is one red, a blend of Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot in American oak that the house calls its emblem (Infonegocios, quoting the house); now so told, and the Nina wines of Valle de Aminga kept.

questions[0]: the key Aminga rested on the 'Aminga range'; now the stem asks which valley name marks a wine of the La Rioja cellar, with Valle de Aminga against Uco, Tulum and Calchaquí, valleys of other provinces.
sources: Winetourism and Wine.com replaced by the RIVAR case study (SciELO) and Enolife.
open: 1905 (directories) against 1921 (the RIVAR study: the Mendoza cellar bought from another family in Luján de Cuyo in that year); founded stays empty and the story keeps the directories' date hedged. The integrator may prefer to cut 1905.

The RIVAR study says the firm took shape at Anillaco in 1998 when its owner bought shares of Bodega Menem S.A. and formed San Huberto with Carlos Menem (1930 to 2021); one source only, and the buyer is living, so not told.

The label wording San Huberto La Rioja Torrontés now rests only on the author's earlier reading of Wine.com, dropped from the sources for the RIVAR study; no house sheet exists to confirm the grape as Torrontés Riojano.

records.place: Vichigasta, Chilecito department, Famatina Valley, La Rioja

wine.name: La Puerta Torrontés
wine.sites: The family's vineyard at Vichigasta, south of Chilecito in the Famatina Valley, at about 1,000 metres, on sandy loam of alluvial origin, with hot, dry summer days and cool nights by the house's account.
wine.making: Made without oak and kept on its lees for about five months before bottling, by the house's sheet for the La Puerta line, which adds texture without the mark of wood; the sheet read gives no detail of the ferment.
wine.glass: Jasmine, honeysuckle and citrus blossom over a crisp palate of citrus peel, by the house's own note and merchants' notes for its Torrontés, dry, with fresh acidity under the scent.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within a year or two of the vintage, while the blossom scent is fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no decanting; a white wine glass with a tulip bowl.

label.means: The house's line of varietal wines, sold under the estate's name.
The family estate of vines and olive groves at Vichigasta in the Famatina Valley.
The province's white grape, here Torrontés Riojano, scented like a sweet wine and finishing dry.

records.table: Valle de la Puerta is a family estate of vines and olive groves at Vichigasta, south of Chilecito, planted from 1994. Its La Puerta Torrontés is unoaked and rested on its lees, scented with jasmine and citrus blossom: a white to pour cold before dinner.
records.story: The house dates its first vines and olive trees to 1994, planted at Vichigasta, south of Chilecito in the Famatina Valley, on land that, by its own account, the Diaguita people farmed centuries before, in a village whose name it says the Incas gave. Its winery followed in 2002 and an olive oil plant in 2005, so the estate sells oil beside its wine, and a spring on the land, Ichanka, which the house translates as water of the condor, gives its name to a range from parcels it sets apart within the vineyard. The province lists the estate among the bodegas of its wine route through Chilecito and the Famatina, and its Torrontés has reached merchants abroad under the La Puerta name. It bottles several lines: La Puerta, the varietal range; La Puerta Alta, with its own Torrontés; Ichanka; and wines of the house's own invention, among them a sweet Torrontés. For a sommelier La Puerta Torrontés is the estate's everyday white, a measure of Famatina Torrontés from one family's vines rather than a co-operative's many growers.

others.name: La Puerta Alta Torrontés
others.note: The Torrontés of the house's Alta line, unoaked by a critic's listing.

others.name: Ichanka
others.note: Wines from parcels the house sets apart within its Vichigasta vineyard, named for a spring on the estate.

others.name: Dulce Natural Torrontés
others.note: The house's sweet Torrontés, a different wine from the dry La Puerta.

traps: La Puerta Torrontés and La Puerta Alta Torrontés are two lines of the same house; read the word Alta on the label.
Vichigasta is in the Chilecito department of La Rioja's Famatina Valley; the estate has no tie to any house of Spain's Rioja.

cards.front: Valle de la Puerta: when does it date its first vines and olive trees?
cards.back: 1994, at Vichigasta in the Famatina Valley.

cards.front: What does Valle de la Puerta make besides wine, and since when?
cards.back: Olive oil, from groves planted with its first vines and pressed in its own plant from 2005.

questions.q: How is Valle de la Puerta's La Puerta Torrontés raised before bottling, by the house's sheet?
opts: In clay jars on its skins
questions.exp: The house's sheet gives no oak and about five months on the lees; new oak, flor and clay jars belong to other wines and other places.

questions.q: In which year did Valle de la Puerta build its winery, by its own account?
questions.exp: The winery followed in 2002; 1994 is the year of the first vines and olive trees, and 2005 the olive oil plant.

sources.title: Valle de la Puerta: Nosotros
Valle de la Puerta: La Puerta line and Viñedos y Bodega
La Rioja Turismo: Bodega Valle de La Puerta
Circuito Gastronómico: how the Valle de la Puerta winery began
FirstLeaf wine directory: La Puerta Torrontés, Famatina Valley

report: 1994 for the first vines and olives, 2002 for the winery and 2005 for the oil plant come from the house's own Nosotros page; 1994 and 2002 are also given by a directory and a press note.
The height: the house says 1,000 metres but gives 2,380 feet beside it, which do not agree; the provincial tourism page says more than 1,000 metres, so the record says about 1,000.
No source read confirms that Torrontés was the first grape the house planted (the plan's why says so); one press note says Syrah was its first red. The claim is left out.

The tasting note rests on merchants' notes (FirstLeaf, the HKTDC listing) for several vintages of La Puerta and La Puerta Alta Torrontés, so it is kept to what they share: jasmine, honeysuckle, citrus blossom and crisp citrus; a critic's note of lime and a viscous texture is left out because the critic's site may not be cited.
The long skin contact Torrontés and the sweet Torrontés rest on Vinetur alone; awards are never told. A white Malbec named by one press note is left out.
The house also bottles Mendoza fruit under La Puerta Alta by a critic's listing; the La Puerta Torrontés is tied to the Famatina by the house's sheet.

changed: story: the Torrontés left long on its skins in the old way rested on Vinetur alone; cut. questions[0].exp no longer cites it.
wine.glass: jasmine, honeysuckle and citrus now rest on the house's own La Puerta page as well as merchants'.
sources[3]: Bottlebooks replaced by Circuito Gastronómico, which gives 1994 for the vines and olives, 2001 to 2002 for the winery and 2005 for the oil plant, independent of the house.
open: The house gives 9 to 12 degrees Celsius to serve; the record keeps the Codex's 8 to 10 for aromatic whites.
One source dates the first plantings to 1995 and ties the start to the national tax deferral law; 1994 kept as the house's year and the majority's.

records.place: Valle de Huaco, Sanagasta department, La Rioja

wine.name: Vista Larga Malbec
wine.grapes: Malbec, as the label names it.
wine.sites: The family's organic farm in the Valle de Huaco, in the department of Sanagasta, on the national road about forty kilometres from the city of La Rioja and some 1,250 metres up, the first extensive planting of its valley by the house's account.
wine.making: Made in the family's small artisan cellar on the farm; no technical sheet was found in the sources read, so the record gives no ferment, vessel or time in wood.
wine.glass: Deep red; plum and black pepper, full bodied and velvety, by the house's own note for its Malbec, which names no oak, unlike its Malbec Reserva raised in French barrels.
wine.ageing: No guidance from the house was found in the sources read; read the vintage on the label and taste before advising a guest.
wine.serve: 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, as the house advises; decant only if the wine shows sediment; a red wine glass of middle size.

label.means: The family farm and organic estate in the Valle de Huaco, its name Spanish for a long view.
The single variety named, the red grape Argentina is known by.

records.table: Vista Larga is a small family farm and organic cellar in the Valle de Huaco, about 1,250 metres up in Sanagasta, a valley recognised as a geographical indication of its own in 2026. Its Malbec, plum and black pepper, is a red of the province from outside the Famatina.
records.story: Huaco is a small valley in the department of Sanagasta, north of the provincial capital, and by the farm's own account the Jesuits once chose its land for their vines, until the order was expelled from the Spanish empire in 1767. Long after them a family planted Torrontés, Chardonnay, Malbec and Bonarda at Vista Larga and began to make them in a small cellar of its own on the farm, where it sells wine, olive oil, olives and walnuts to visitors on the national road through the valley; the province lists the farm on its wine tourism route. The firm behind it, San Miguel Arcángel, asked the national wine institute to protect the valley's name, and by its resolution 6 of 2026, published on 22 October 2026, the institute recognised Huaco, with Valle de Huaco as its synonym, as a geographical indication of Argentina in the department of Sanagasta. For a sommelier Vista Larga is a house to know as the whole of a new indication: one family's vines in a valley that it planted afresh, and a Malbec of the province grown away from the Famatina.

report: The thinnest of the five, as the plan warned: no house site was found, so the making, the glass and the ageing say plainly that no sheet or note was found rather than guess.

The geographical indication is confirmed from the resolution itself (RESOL 2026 6 APN INV, dated 16 October 2026, read through search of the copy at cda.org.ar): Huaco, with Valle de Huaco as synonym, Sanagasta, on the application of San Miguel Arcángel S.A.; a Nueva Rioja note gives Vista Larga Malbec as a wine of Bodega San Miguel Arcángel, which ties the firm to the farm.
The Jesuit vines rest on Bichos de Campo alone and are hedged as its account; 1767 is the expulsion of the Jesuits from the Spanish empire, a date of general history.

The grapes (Torrontés, Chardonnay, Malbec, Bonarda) rest on Bichos de Campo and Vivino; the organic claim rests on one press note and is left out, and awards are never told. No founding year was found; founded is empty.
The others names are given as Vivino and the press list them; the integrator may wish to confirm the label wording.

Swap to weigh: no better sourced house was found on the province's wine route (Las Flechas Group and Concepción Viñedos Sustentables of Chilecito appear there, no better known); the pick stands as a thin region house, told plainly.

changed: story: the INV resolution 6 of 16 October 2026 now 'resolution 6 of 2026, published on 22 October 2026' (Ámbito, La Posta, DataPortuaria); the signing date of 16 October was not confirmed by a second reading. questions[1].exp likewise.

wine.sites, table, story: 'the one planting of its valley' was the press's; the house's own page says the first extensive planting in the valley, so the sites say so hedged as the house's, and the table and story no longer claim it.
story: the Jesuit vines now the farm's own account (vistalarga.com.ar); 'four centuries after them' was wrong in sum (the expulsion was 1767), now 'long after them'.

wine.glass and wine.serve: no note was found by the author; the house's own Malbec page gives plum and black pepper, full bodied and velvety, no oak named, and 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, now given as the house's.

Vista Larga is the farm and San Miguel Arcángel S.A. the applicant for the indication; the tie between them rests on one Nueva Rioja note.
